one_liner: no_std Rust CBOR codec whose derived encoders serialize 2.6-6.9x faster than rmp-serde (MessagePack); decoding is only on par.
what_it_does: A CBOR (RFC 8949) encoder and decoder for Rust, built to work in no_std. You derive its own Encode/Decode traits (from minicbor-derive) and give every field and enum variant an integer index such as #[n(0)]. You can also drive Encoder/Decoder by hand, iterate over a token stream, or get the encoded size up front through CborLen. It is not a serde format by default. The separate minicbor-serde crate adds a serde Serializer/Deserializer, but it keeps field names as strings, and the benchmark did not measure it.
how_it_is_fast: It uses no special algorithm. The derived code calls concrete, type-specific Encoder/Decoder methods (Encoder::str, Decoder::u32) directly, with no serde Serializer/Visitor layer in between. The Encoder writes into a caller-supplied &mut [u8] or Vec<u8> using copy_from_slice/extend_from_slice and allocates nothing. The derive replaces field names with integer indices and by default encodes a struct as a CBOR array where position stands for the index, so no string keys are written or matched; &str and ByteSlice fields decode zero-copy from the input after UTF-8 checking. The benchmark does not show which of these produces the gap over rmp-serde.
when_to_use: Encode-heavy paths such as logging, telemetry or snapshots now on rmp-serde. On all four shootout datasets, serialize time drops 2.6x (minecraft_savedata) to 6.9x (mesh), and 3.2x on string-heavy log records.

You already use CBOR through ciborium. On log it is ~8.3x faster to serialize and ~4.6x faster to deserialize, and the output is ~42% smaller (817,830 vs 1,407,835 bytes) because integer indices replace field names. Against cbor4ii, deserialize is ~1.8x faster and serialize is close (405.77 vs 471.14 us).
no_std or embedded targets. The core crate has no required dependencies, encodes into a fixed &mut [u8] without allocating, and CI builds it for aarch64-unknown-none.

Long-lived or cross-language data where you want a standard, self-describing format with protobuf-style evolution: unknown fields are skipped, a missing Option decodes as None, and indices let you rename freely.
Read paths that can borrow. Decoding into &str or ByteSlice borrows from the input: 1.0694 ms on log vs 2.3448 ms for owned decoding.
when_not_to_use: Decode-dominated workloads. Deserialize ranges from ~13% slower than rmp-serde (minecraft_savedata 2.6924 vs 2.3727 ms) to ~5% faster (mk48), so reads gain nothing.
You must emit MessagePack, or just want the fastest Rust MessagePack. msgpacker and zerompk beat it on the same log table (serialize ~266-269 us, deserialize 1.81-2.07 ms).
You need deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949 section 4.2) for hashing or signing. Floats are always written at their declared width and map keys are not sorted; the request is open as issue #58.
You want to keep plain serde derives. The measured numbers come from the native #[derive(Encode, Decode)] with #[n(i)] on every field, and minicbor-serde's speed is not in this benchmark.
Your toolchain is older than Rust 1.85 (the crate uses edition 2024; the maintainer declined 2021 support in #50), or your policy only allows MIT/Apache (the maintainer declined relicensing in #6).

integration.dependencies: none required; optional minicbor-derive (a proc-macro built on syn/quote/proc-macro2) via the 'derive' feature, 'half' for f16; minicbor-serde adds serde
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 (edition 2024). Cargo.toml has no rust-version field, and CI tests only stable and beta.
integration.platforms: any; no_std core (CI builds for aarch64-unknown-none); 'alloc' and 'std' features add collections and std types; atomic impls are gated on target_has_atomic
integration.thread_safety: not documented; Encoder and Decoder are plain per-call values (a writer, or a borrowed slice plus a position) with no global state

gotchas: Every field and variant needs an explicit index. The default array encoding writes a NULL byte for each None and each index gap, so use #[cbor(map)] for sparse types. Non-optional fields can never be removed, and a top-level enum is not forward-compatible: an unknown variant is an error unless the enum sits behind an Option field.
&[u8] and Vec<u8> encode as CBOR arrays of integers, not byte strings, unless you use ByteSlice/ByteVec or #[cbor(with = "minicbor::bytes")].
Without the 'alloc' feature, Decoder::skip cannot skip indefinite-length arrays or maps nested inside definite ones. An unknown field of that shape then fails decoding instead of being ignored.

minicbor-serde's Deserializer reports is_human_readable = false. Serde internally tagged enums holding types such as SocketAddr then fail to round-trip (issue #55, closed as a serde upstream problem).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick minicbor over postcard (366.95 us serialize on the same log table, about the same speed) or bitcode (96.821 us) when the bytes must be standard CBOR that other languages' decoders can read, with index-based field evolution. If the data never leaves Rust and throughput is the goal, bitcode, serde-zap, wincode and rkyv all post much faster serialize times on the same page.
verified_claims_summary: Source: djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark run of 2026-09-10 (Criterion; rustc 1.100.0-nightly, LLVM 23.1.1, bench profile with LTO; AMD EPYC 9V74, 4 vCPUs, Hyper-V guest). On the log dataset, minicbor 2.3.0 with derived Encode/Decode serialized into a preallocated slice in 405.77 us vs 1.3179 ms for rmp-serde 1.3.1 (~3.2x), and deserialized in 2.3448 vs 2.3829 ms (a tie). The same run puts it ~8.3x ahead of ciborium 0.2.2 on serialize and ~4.6x on deserialize.
